narration: A hydrothermal vent is an opening in the seafloor where seawater that has soaked down into hot rock flows back out, heated and loaded with dissolved minerals.
NOAA puts the hottest of that fluid at up to 400 degrees Celsius, and on the deep seafloor it stays liquid.
That number tells you how hot a vent can run. It does not tell you why the water refuses to boil, where the heat comes from, or how whole communities of animals live beside it in total darkness.
Those answers were assembled piece by piece, from instruments, samples, and one discovery nobody planned for.
What is a hydrothermal vent?

Vents were expected before they were found. By the time of the first expedition, the theory of seafloor spreading held that new ocean crust forms along mid-ocean ridges, where tectonic plates pull apart and molten rock rises close to the seafloor.
If that was right, cold ocean water should be seeping into the young, cracked rock, warming up, and escaping somewhere.
Instruments towed above the Galápagos Rift had recorded faint pulses of warmer water.
So in 1977, scientists dove in the submersible Alvin, operated by the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, to find the source.
They found the warm springs. Around them they also found something the expedition had not been designed to study: dense clusters of clams, mussels and tube worms, thriving in the dark.
The team was made up mostly of geologists and geochemists, and the biology arrived as a surprise.
Two years later, in 1979, Alvin dives on the East Pacific Rise found something hotter.
Tall mineral chimneys were pouring out what looked like thick black smoke.
The temperature probe the team carried was not built for it; by WHOI's account, part of it melted.
Those first black smokers turned a predicted phenomenon into one of the most closely studied features of the deep ocean.
Here is the sequence as geochemists reconstruct it. First, cold seawater seeps down through cracks in the crust near a ridge.
Deeper in, that water is heated by magma sitting below the seafloor.

Hot water under pressure is chemically aggressive. As it moves through rock it gives up some of its own dissolved ingredients and dissolves metals and sulfide in their place: iron, copper, zinc, and hydrogen sulfide among them.
Hot fluid is buoyant, so it rises and exits through the seafloor, often along the same fractures that let it in.
When that fluid meets bottom water just above freezing, much of what it carries precipitates almost instantly.
That is what the black smoke is. NOAA describes it as a cloud of mineral particles, mostly metal sulfides, not smoke in any burning sense.
Some of those particles settle around the opening, and layer by layer they build a hollow chimney.
Chimneys grow, crack, topple and regrow. Where hot fluid has already mixed with seawater underground, the vent runs cooler, carries lighter-colored minerals, and is called a white smoker.
Other vents build no chimney at all. They appear only as shimmering water rising from cracks, called diffuse flow.
No one has watched seawater travel down through the crust, so that leg of the loop is inferred.
The strongest evidence is chemical. Vent fluid collected by submersibles and robotic vehicles comes up almost stripped of magnesium, an element seawater normally carries in abundance.
The simplest explanation is that the water reacted with hot rock along the way and left its magnesium behind in new minerals.
Seismic surveys that image magma beneath ridges, and laboratory experiments that heat seawater with crushed basalt, point to the same loop.
At sea level, pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. That is not a property of water alone.
It is a property of water under the weight of one atmosphere of air.
On the deep seafloor, the whole ocean above presses down, and the pressure there is many times higher than at the surface.
The boiling point is set by pressure, and it climbs with it.
That is why fluid near 400 degrees can leave a chimney as a liquid rather than as a burst of steam.

Pressure raises the bar, but it does not remove it. Under some combinations of temperature and depth, vent fluid does boil underground, or separates into a lighter, vapor-like phase and a dense, salty brine.
Scientists detect this after the fact, in the saltiness of what comes out.
Some vents release fluid fresher than seawater and others release fluid saltier than seawater, and that difference is a fingerprint of separation happening somewhere below.
At the hottest and deepest extremes, the distinction between liquid and gas stops being meaningful at all.
Almost every food web you know begins with photosynthesis. Sunlight fades quickly with depth, and at most vents there is none at all.

Life there runs instead on chemosynthesis. Microbes capture energy from chemical reactions, most famously by oxidizing the hydrogen sulfide in vent fluid, and use that energy to build sugars from carbon dioxide.
Some live free in the water or on rock. Others live inside animals.
Either way, these microbes are the base of the vent food web.
The giant tube worm, Riftia pachyptila, shows how far that partnership can go.
Adults have no mouth and no gut. Their red plume, colored by hemoglobin, takes up oxygen, carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide from the surrounding water.
The blood carries those to an organ called the trophosome, packed with symbiotic bacteria that run the chemistry and feed the worm from within.
The animal itself lives inside a tough white tube anchored to the rock.
Biologists did not take that arrangement on trust. Several lines of evidence agree.
Dissection showed there is no mouth and no gut. Microscopy showed bacteria inside the trophosome, densely packed in its cells.
Enzyme measurements found the chemical machinery for fixing carbon using energy from sulfide.
And carbon signatures in the worm's tissue match carbon fixed by those bacteria, not carbon from food sinking down from the surface.
Any one of these could be questioned on its own. Together, they show the worm is fed by its symbionts.
Vent communities also differ from ocean to ocean. Giant tube worms dominate many Pacific sites.
On the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, swarming shrimp crowd the chimneys instead. In the Indian Ocean, the scaly-foot snail grows a shell layered with iron sulfide.
Biologists explain these differences partly by how larvae disperse between vent fields that can be far apart, and partly by local chemistry.
How exactly animals colonize a newly formed vent remains an active question.
Black smokers are not the whole story. In 2000, researchers exploring near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge came upon a field of pale, towering chimneys that became known as Lost City.

NOAA Ocean Exploration has documented the site with remotely operated vehicles. Its chimneys are made of carbonate minerals, not metal sulfides, and its fluid is far cooler than a black smoker's and strongly alkaline rather than acidic.
The heat source is different too. Lost City sits on mantle rock that has been pushed up close to the seafloor.
When seawater reacts with that rock, in a process called serpentinization, the reaction itself releases heat, along with hydrogen and methane.
So Lost City is driven by rock chemistry, not driven by magma.
That matters because it means vents can exist away from active volcanic centers, and it gives microbes a different menu of chemical energy to live on.

Vents also affect the ocean as a whole. Seawater is thought to circulate through hydrothermal systems over very long timescales, and in the process vents add some elements to the ocean and remove others.
Plumes of dissolved iron from vents have been traced far from their source.
The minerals left behind form deposits rich in copper, zinc and other metals, which is why vents interest economic geologists as well as biologists.
Much of this work is published by public bodies: NOAA reports on vent temperatures and expeditions, WHOI on Alvin and the 1977 dives, and the Smithsonian on deep-sea life.
Vents also sit at the center of one of science's open questions.

Some researchers propose that life on Earth began at hydrothermal vents, where chemical energy and mineral surfaces were both available, and alkaline systems like Lost City feature heavily in that argument.
Others favor shallow pools on land, where repeated drying and wetting can concentrate molecules.
Laboratory experiments support pieces of both ideas. Neither has been demonstrated, and you should treat any confident claim either way as ahead of the evidence.
Space is fascinating, but Earth bothers me more. We're already here and still don't understand huge parts of it.
As you watch vent footage, remember that every image is lit by the vehicle itself.
Without its lamps the scene would be black, so the colors you see are the colors of artificial light on rock and tissue.
The black smoke looks slow and soft, but it is fluid hot enough to damage instruments not built for it.

Watch, too, for the shimmer above the cooler cracks. That ripple is diffuse flow, warm water bending the light as it rises, and many vent animals live in that milder water rather than in the hottest jets.
This evidence firmly establishes some things. First, vent fluid stays liquid under pressure, which follows from basic physics and is confirmed by direct measurement.
Second, tube worms are fed by symbionts, shown by several independent lines of evidence.
Other things remain open. No one knows precisely how many vents exist.
The mid-ocean ridge system is enormous, only a small fraction has been surveyed closely, and estimates vary widely.
Vents can switch on and off as eruptions and earthquakes reshape the plumbing, so any map is a snapshot.
And where life began is not settled by anything in this video.
A hydrothermal vent is seawater returning from a journey through hot rock, carrying the crust's chemistry back into the ocean.
We know its temperature because instruments were sent into it, its plumbing because of what is missing from its water, and its life because biologists took that life apart and looked.
Much of the seafloor where such vents could exist has still never been seen.
